questions.question: What is Terraform and what problem does it solve?
questions.answer: Infrastructure as Code tool by HashiCorp. Declarative — describe desired state, Terraform figures out how. Provider-agnostic (AWS, GCP, Azure, K8s). Solves: manual infra drift, undocumented changes, non-reproducible environments, snowflake servers.

questions.question: Explain the Terraform workflow: init, plan, apply, destroy.
questions.answer: The workflow includes the following stages. First: download providers, initialise backend, install modules. Second: compare desired vs current state, show diff — no changes made. Third: executes the plan, updates state. Fourth: plans and applies deletion of all resources. Always review plan before applying.
bestPractices: Always review the plan before running apply.

questions.question: What is the difference between declarative and imperative IaC?
questions.answer: Declarative: describe what you want (Terraform, CloudFormation) — tool determines how. Imperative: describe how to do it (Ansible, bash) — you control order. Terraform is declarative. Benefits: idempotent, self-documenting, convergent — running apply twice is safe.

questions.question: What happens during terraform init?
questions.answer: Downloads provider plugins from the first block. Initialises backend (S3, local). Downloads modules from registry or local path. Creates .terraform directory and .terraform.lock.hcl for provider version pinning. Safe to run multiple times — idempotent.

questions.question: What is a Terraform provider?
questions.answer: Plugin translating Terraform config into API calls for a specific platform. AWS provider wraps AWS APIs. Each provider has its own resources and data sources. Versioned independently — pin provider versions in the following block. HashiCorp, community, and custom providers available.
bestPractices: Always pin provider versions in required_providers block.

questions.question: What is the difference between terraform plan and terraform apply?
questions.answer: The first command: read-only, shows what would change (+/-/~), writes to plan file if the first flag is specified, no state changes. The second command: executes changes, updates state. Always use the second option in CI — apply that exact plan file to prevent drift between plan and apply in automation.
bestPractices: Always use -out=tfplan in CI and apply that exact plan file to prevent drift between plan and apply stages.

questions.question: What is idempotency in Terraform?
questions.answer: Running apply multiple times on unchanged config produces no changes. Terraform compares desired state (config) vs actual state (state file + API refresh). Only differing resources are changed. Critical for CI/CD — safe to run apply on every merge if config unchanged.

questions.question: What is terraform fmt and terraform validate?
questions.answer: fmt: formats .tf files to canonical HCL style — run in CI to enforce formatting. validate: checks syntax and internal consistency (references, types) without API calls. Neither checks if resources actually exist — that's plan's job. Both should run in pre-commit hooks.
bestPractices: Run terraform fmt and terraform validate in pre-commit hooks and CI pipelines.

questions.question: What is the .terraform.lock.hcl file?
questions.answer: Records exact provider versions and checksums selected during init. Commit to Git — ensures all team members and CI use identical provider versions. Update using the following command. Never manually edit. Like package-lock.json for providers.
bestPractices: Commit .terraform.lock.hcl to Git to ensure consistent provider versions across all environments.
warnings: Never manually edit .terraform.lock.hcl.

questions.question: What is terraform refresh and when would you use it?
questions.answer: Syncs state file with actual infrastructure — updates state without changing infra. Rarely needed explicitly — terraform plan does implicit refresh. Use when manual changes made outside Terraform need to be reflected in state. Deprecated in favour of the following flag.
warnings: terraform refresh is deprecated in favour of the -refresh-only flag.

questions.question: What is the difference between terraform apply and terraform apply -auto-approve?
questions.answer: The first option skips interactive confirmation. Never use in production pipelines without plan file review. Pattern: run the second command, human review, then run the third command. The first option is acceptable in dev/test automation only — never production.
warnings: Never use -auto-approve in production pipelines without plan file review.

questions.question: What is the Terraform registry?
questions.answer: Public registry at registry.terraform.io for providers and modules. Versioned, documented, HashiCorp-verified. Reference modules using the following attribute. Private registry in Terraform Cloud/Enterprise. Always pin module versions — never use latest implicitly.
bestPractices: Always pin module versions; never use latest implicitly.

questions.question: What is Terraform state and why does it exist?
questions.answer: JSON file mapping config resources to real-world infrastructure IDs. Tracks metadata, dependencies, resource attributes. Required because APIs don't know about Terraform — state bridges the gap. Without state: can't know what exists, can't detect drift, can't determine correct update order.

questions.question: What are the risks of local state in a team environment?
questions.answer: No locking: two simultaneous applies corrupt state. No sharing: team members have different state. No backup: local file lost = Terraform loses track of all infrastructure. No audit trail. Solution: always use remote backend (S3 + DynamoDB) from day one.
bestPractices: Always use a remote backend (S3 + DynamoDB) from day one in a team environment.

questions.question: How do you configure an S3 remote backend with locking?
questions.answer: Use the following configuration block. DynamoDB lock prevents concurrent applies. Enable versioning on S3 bucket for state history. Separate state bucket per environment.
bestPractices: Enable versioning on the S3 bucket used for state history.
Use a separate state bucket per environment.

questions.question: What is state locking and what happens if a lock is stuck?
questions.answer: DynamoDB item written at apply start, deleted at end. Stuck lock: apply crashed mid-run. Force unlock using the following command. Verify no apply is actually running before force unlocking — data corruption risk if applied concurrently. Check CloudTrail for who started the locked apply.
warnings: Force unlocking while an apply is active can lead to data corruption.

questions.question: What does terraform state list do?
questions.answer: Lists all resources tracked in state file. Use to: verify what Terraform manages, find resource address for targeted operations. Combined with the second command: displays full attributes. Never read state file directly with the third command — always use CLI commands.
warnings: Never read the state file directly (e.g. with cat); always use the CLI commands.

questions.question: What is terraform state mv and when do you use it?
questions.answer: Moves resource in state without destroying/recreating. Use cases: renaming a resource, moving into/out of module, reorganising code. Example: the following command. Always run plan after state mv to verify no unintended changes. Critical for refactoring without downtime.
bestPractices: Always run terraform plan after a state mv operation to verify that no unintended replacements are scheduled.

questions.question: What is terraform state rm?
questions.answer: Removes resource from state — Terraform forgets it but does NOT destroy the actual resource. Use when: resource should no longer be managed by Terraform, cleaning up after manual deletion. Resource stays running — just untracked. Complement with the second configuration option.

questions.question: What is terraform import?
questions.answer: Brings existing resource into state. Example: the first command. Adds to state but does NOT generate .tf config — must write matching config manually. After import: plan should show no changes. New: the second configuration block in config (v1.5+).

questions.question: How do you handle state file corruption?
questions.answer: S3 versioning: restore previous version. Run the first command before risky operations. If inconsistent with reality: run the second command to resync. Last resort: terraform state commands — never raw JSON edits. Prevention: locking + versioning + backup.
warnings: As a last resort, use terraform state commands; never make raw JSON edits to the state file.

questions.question: What is a partial state and how does it occur?
questions.answer: Apply interrupted mid-run (crash, timeout, CTRL+C). Some resources created, state partially updated. Resolution: run terraform plan — Terraform reconciles partial state. May need terraform import for resources created but not in state. Always let apply complete when possible.
bestPractices: Always let the apply step complete fully when possible to prevent partial states.

questions.question: What is state isolation and why is it important?
questions.answer: Separate state files per environment (dev/staging/prod). Prevents prod apply from affecting dev state. Implemented via: separate S3 keys per env, separate backends per workspace, or separate Terraform roots. Never share state between prod and non-prod — blast radius containment.
warnings: Never share state between production and non-production environments.

questions.question: What is the terraform_remote_state data source?
questions.answer: Reads outputs from another Terraform state file. Enables cross-stack references: networking stack outputs VPC ID → app stack reads it. Creates tight coupling between stacks. Alternative: SSM Parameter Store for looser coupling. Use carefully — change in one stack can break dependent stacks.
warnings: Use carefully; changes in one stack can break dependent stacks due to tight coupling.

questions.question: What are the types of Terraform variables?
questions.answer: Input variables (var.*): parameters, set via tfvars/env vars/CLI. Local values (local.*): computed values within config, not exposed externally. Output values: expose values from module or root for external use or cross-stack sharing. Variables have type constraints and validation blocks.

questions.question: What is variable precedence in Terraform?
questions.answer: Highest to lowest: the first flag > the second env vars > terraform.tfvars.json > the third file > *.auto.tfvars (alphabetical) > default values. Environment variables useful in CI. Never commit sensitive values in tfvars — use the second env vars format or Secrets Manager.
bestPractices: Use TF_VAR_ environment variables or AWS Secrets Manager for passing sensitive variables.
warnings: Never commit sensitive values in tfvars files.

questions.question: What is the difference between a variable default and nullable?
questions.answer: The first setting defines the value used when not provided — makes variable optional. The second setting ensures the variable must be set and cannot be null. The third setting (default) allows it to be explicitly set to null. Type constraints enforce shape. Validation blocks add custom error messages for invalid values.

questions.question: What are locals and when to use them over variables?
questions.answer: locals: computed values within a module, not settable from outside. Use for: DRY — reference complex expression once, name computed values for clarity, build maps/lists from variables. Not overridable unlike input variables. Common: locals for tags, name prefixes, computed CIDR blocks.

questions.question: What is a data source and how does it differ from a resource?
questions.answer: Data source: reads existing infrastructure (read-only), no state management. Resource: creates/manages infrastructure, tracked in state. Data source refreshed on every plan. Use for: AMIs by filter, existing VPCs, secrets from Secrets Manager. Never use data sources for values you manage with Terraform.
warnings: Never use data sources to query values that you are managing within the same Terraform configuration.

questions.question: How do outputs work and what are they used for?
questions.answer: Expose values from a module or root config. In module: consumed by calling module via module.name.output_name. In root: displayed after apply, readable by the first command, accessible via terraform_remote_state. Mark the second setting for secrets — hides from CLI output but still in state file.

questions.question: What is the sensitive attribute on variables and outputs?
questions.answer: The following setting redacts the value in plan/apply output. Does NOT encrypt in state file — state still contains plaintext. Use for: passwords, API keys, certificates. Protect state file with KMS encryption independently. Anyone with state file access can read sensitive values regardless.
bestPractices: Protect the state file with KMS encryption independently to secure sensitive values.
warnings: sensitive = true does NOT encrypt the state file; plaintext values are still stored in the state.

questions.question: How do you pass complex types as variables?
questions.answer: Type constraints: the following. In tfvars: list = ['a','b'], map = {key='value'}. Use object() for structured config. Avoid any type — loses type safety. Validate with validation blocks for allowed values and format checking.
warnings: Avoid using 'any' type since it loses type safety.

questions.question: What is variable validation?
questions.answer: The following block configuration inside a variable: condition (expression returning bool) + error_message. Runs at plan time before API calls. Example: validate CIDR format, enum of allowed regions, string length. Better than runtime API errors — fails fast with clear message. Always validate inputs to shared modules.
bestPractices: Always validate inputs to shared modules to fail-fast before cloud API calls.

questions.question: What is a Terraform module and why use them?
questions.answer: Reusable encapsulated collection of resources. Root module: your working directory. Child modules: called from root or other modules. Benefits: DRY, consistency, tested abstractions, versioning. A well-designed module hides complexity and exposes only the interface callers need.

questions.question: What is module composition vs inheritance?
questions.answer: Terraform has no inheritance. Composition: modules call other modules, passing outputs as inputs. Wrapper modules: thin module calling community module with opinionated defaults. Build narrow interfaces — only expose variables that legitimately differ between uses.
bestPractices: Build narrow interfaces exposing only variables that legitimately differ between module executions.

questions.question: How do you version a module?
questions.answer: Git tags: source = 'git::https://github.com/org/module.git?ref=v1.2.0'. Registry: source = 'org/module/aws', version = '~> 1.2'. Local path: source = '../modules/vpc' (no versioning — development only). Always pin versions in production. Semantic versioning: major = breaking change.
bestPractices: Always pin module versions in production.
Follow Semantic Versioning (SemVer) strictly.

questions.question: What are module input and output contracts?
questions.answer: Inputs: declared variables with types, descriptions, defaults, validation. Outputs: declared outputs with descriptions, sensitive flag. Module interface should be stable — changes require version bump. Document every variable and output. Think of modules as APIs with contracts — breaking changes need major version bump.
bestPractices: Document every variable and output in modules.
Treat modules as APIs with stable contracts.

questions.question: What is the for_each meta-argument on a module?
questions.answer: Instantiates module multiple times from a map or set. Each instance keyed by map key: module.name[key]. Use for: identical environments (dev/staging), multiple clusters. Cleaner than count — instances have meaningful keys not just indices. Removing item from map destroys that module instance.
bestPractices: Use for_each instead of count for instantiating modules as it provides meaningful keys instead of numerical indices.

questions.question: How do you refactor a module without destroying resources?
questions.answer: Use terraform state mv to move resources to new module paths. Before: aws_instance.web. After: module.web.aws_instance.this. State mv updates tracking without touching real infra. Then run plan — should show no changes. Test in non-prod first. Document steps for teammates. Use moved block (v1.1+) as declarative alternative.
bestPractices: Use the moved block (v1.1+) as a declarative alternative for refactoring.
Test state moves in non-production environments first.

questions.question: What is a module registry and private registry?
questions.answer: Public: registry.terraform.io. Verified: HashiCorp-verified. Private: Terraform Cloud/Enterprise — internal modules with versioning and access control. Alternative: Git repo with version tags. Review public modules before using in production — don't blindly trust community code.
warnings: Don't blindly trust community code; review public modules before using them in production.

questions.question: What is the difference between module source types?
questions.answer: Local: '../modules/vpc' — no version, for development. Git: 'git::https://...' with ref tag. Registry: 'hashicorp/consul/aws' with version. HTTP URL: direct download. S3: 'S3::bucket/module.zip'. Prefer registry or Git with pinned version for shared modules. Local for in-repo modules only.
bestPractices: Prefer using a registry or Git repository with pinned versions for shared modules.
Use local paths only for in-repository modules.

questions.question: How do you test a Terraform module?
questions.answer: Terratest (Go): provisions real infra, runs assertions, destroys. terraform test (native, v1.6+): .tftest.hcl files, mock providers. Checkov/tfsec: static analysis for security misconfigs. terraform validate: syntax. Plan output review. Always test in isolated account — never in production.
warnings: Always test in an isolated test account; never in production.

questions.question: What makes a good module interface design?
questions.answer: Minimal surface area: expose only variables that legitimately vary. Sensible defaults: caller shouldn't set everything. Typed inputs: catch errors early. Documented outputs. Opinionated defaults: module enforces best practices (encryption on, logging on). Single responsibility: VPC module does VPC only.
bestPractices: Enforce single responsibility: a VPC module should do VPC only.
Design opinionated defaults enforcing security and logging.

questions.question: What are meta-arguments in Terraform?
questions.answer: Special arguments available on all resources regardless of provider: depends_on, count, for_each, provider, lifecycle. Not provider-specific — built into Terraform language. lifecycle controls create/destruction behaviour. count and for_each enable resource multiplication.

questions.question: What is the lifecycle block and its options?
questions.answer: create_before_destroy: create replacement before destroying old. prevent_destroy: block any destroy operation (use for prod DBs). ignore_changes: ignore diffs in specified attributes. replace_triggered_by: force replacement when another resource changes. Each solves a specific operational need.
bestPractices: Use prevent_destroy for critical production resources like databases.

questions.question: When would you use create_before_destroy?
questions.answer: Resources where downtime is unacceptable: ALB, RDS, certificate. Without it: Terraform destroys then creates — gap in service. With it: new resource created, references updated, old destroyed. Requires resource accepts duplicate existence temporarily. Pair with random_id suffix to avoid name conflicts.
bestPractices: Pair create_before_destroy with a random_id suffix on resource names to avoid duplicate name conflicts during rollouts.

questions.question: What is prevent_destroy and its limitations?
questions.answer: Blocks any plan that would destroy the resource. Protects against accidental terraform destroy. Limitation: only prevents Terraform-initiated destroy — doesn't stop AWS Console deletion. Remove prevent_destroy from config to actually destroy. Use for: RDS, S3 buckets with data, KMS keys.
warnings: prevent_destroy only prevents Terraform-initiated deletions; it cannot stop manual console-based deletions.

questions.question: What is ignore_changes and when to use it?
questions.answer: Ignores diffs in specific attributes — won't show as change in plan. Use for: attributes managed externally (ASG desired count), initial passwords rotated externally, tags added by other tools. Don't overuse — masks real drift. Good use: lifecycle { ignore_changes = [tags] } for tag exceptions.
warnings: Don't overuse ignore_changes as it masks real infrastructure drift.

questions.question: What is the difference between count and for_each?
questions.answer: count: integer, instances addressed by index [0]. for_each: map or set, instances addressed by key ['dev']. Problem with count: removing middle element renumbers all subsequent — Terraform destroys and recreates rest. for_each: removing a key only affects that instance. Always prefer for_each for production resources.
bestPractices: Always prefer for_each over count for production resources to avoid array index renumbering issues.
warnings: Removing elements from a list using count will trigger replacements of all subsequent resources in the array due to index shifts.

questions.question: What is depends_on and when is it necessary?
questions.answer: Explicit dependency when Terraform can't infer from references. Example: IAM policy must be attached before EC2 uses it — but EC2 config doesn't reference policy. Use sparingly — overuse slows graph parallelism. If using depends_on often, resource references are probably missing.
warnings: Use depends_on sparingly as it blocks parallel resource execution pipelines.

questions.question: What is the replace_triggered_by lifecycle argument?
questions.answer: Forces resource replacement when referenced resource or value changes. Example: force EC2 replacement when launch template changes. Useful for: immutable infrastructure patterns, triggering node rollouts. Requires Terraform 1.2+. More explicit than taint.

questions.question: What is the moved block in Terraform?
questions.answer: Declarative way to record a resource moved to a new address. Terraform updates state to match without destroying/recreating. Committed to config — communicates change to team. Supersedes terraform state mv for most cases. Available since Terraform 1.1. After next apply, moved block can be removed.
bestPractices: Use declarative moved blocks instead of imperative terraform state mv to trace code refactoring across team repositories.

questions.question: What are the most useful Terraform built-in functions?
questions.answer: String: format(), join(), split(), trimspace(). Collection: length(), lookup(), merge(), flatten(), toset(). Type: tostring(), tonumber(). Encoding: jsonencode(), yamldecode(), base64encode(). File: file(), templatefile(). Conditional: coalesce(), coalescelist(). Functions are pure — no side effects.

questions.question: What is the ternary conditional expression?
questions.answer: condition ? true_val : false_val. Example: var.env == 'prod' ? 'db.r5.large' : 'db.t3.small'. Can be nested but avoid deep nesting — use locals for readability. Common use: environment-specific values, conditional enabling with count = var.enable ? 1 : 0.
bestPractices: Avoid deep nesting of ternary operators; use locals instead to preserve readability.

questions.question: What is a dynamic block?
questions.answer: Generates repeated nested blocks from a collection. Replaces copy-pasted repeated blocks (ingress rules, lifecycle rules). dynamic 'ingress' iterates var.ingress_rules, content block defines each iteration. Good for: SG rules, S3 lifecycle rules, IAM policy statements. Don't overuse — reduces readability.
warnings: Don't overuse dynamic blocks as they reduce HCL readability significantly.

questions.question: What is templatefile() and when do you use it?
questions.answer: Renders a template file with variables substituted. templatefile('userdata.sh.tpl', {cluster_name = var.name}). Template uses ${variable} syntax. Use for: EC2 user data, K8s manifests, config files varying per environment. Better than heredoc for complex multi-line templates. File read at plan time.
bestPractices: Use templatefile() instead of inline heredocs for complex user data scripts or configuration templates.

questions.question: What is the for expression in Terraform?
questions.answer: [for item in list : expression] or {for k, v in map : k => expression}. Transforms collections. Example: [for s in var.subnets : upper(s)]. Filter with if: [for s in var.subnets : s if s.public]. Returns list or map. Powerful for data transformation without external tools.

codeBlocks.code: [for s in var.subnets : s if s.public]

questions.question: What is the splat expression?
questions.answer: aws_instance.web[*].id — shorthand for [for i in aws_instance.web : i.id]. Works with count-based resources. Returns list of attribute values. Does NOT work with for_each — use values(aws_instance.web)[*].id or for expression instead. Useful for passing all instance IDs to another resource.
warnings: Splat expressions ([*]) do NOT work with resources created using for_each; use values(resource)[*].attribute instead.

questions.question: How do you handle null and optional values?
questions.answer: null: represents absence of value. coalesce(var.custom, 'default'): returns first non-null. can(): returns bool if expression succeeds. try(): returns first successful expression. optional() in object type: marks attribute optional with default. Handle nulls explicitly — unexpected nulls cause cryptic errors.
bestPractices: Handle null values explicitly to avoid cryptic Terraform runtime errors.

questions.question: What is jsonencode() used for in Terraform?
questions.answer: Converts HCL value to JSON string. Essential for: IAM policies, ECS task definitions, K8s annotations. Better than heredoc JSON — HCL variables interpolated, validated at plan time, formatted properly. Pair with jsondecode() to parse JSON from data sources. Use for all inline JSON in Terraform.
bestPractices: Use jsonencode() instead of inline heredocs for creating IAM policies or JSON payloads; this validates JSON syntax at plan time.

questions.question: What are type constraints in Terraform?
questions.answer: Primitive: string, number, bool. Collection: list(type), set(type), map(type). Structural: object({attr=type}), tuple([type,type]). any: disables type checking. Type constraints on variables catch mismatches at plan time. Always use specific types — avoid any except in wrapper modules accepting arbitrary shapes.
bestPractices: Always specify strict variable types; avoid 'any' to ensure plan-time configuration validation.

questions.question: What is the lookup() function and its alternative?
questions.answer: lookup(map, key, default): returns value or default if key missing. Example: lookup(var.instance_types, var.env, 't3.micro'). Alternative: var.instance_types[var.env] (errors if missing) or try(var.instance_types[var.env], 't3.micro'). Prefer direct indexing with validation for better error messages.
bestPractices: Prefer direct indexing with try() over lookup() for better error feedback and type verification.

questions.question: What is a Terraform workspace?
questions.answer: Named isolated state within a single backend. terraform workspace new prod creates prod state. terraform.workspace variable returns current name. Default workspace always exists. Limitation: same code for all workspaces — hard to have truly different configs. Not recommended for strong environment isolation.
warnings: Workspaces are not recommended for strong environment isolation (e.g. separating prod and non-prod).

questions.question: Workspaces vs separate directories for environment management?
questions.answer: Workspaces: single codebase, separate state. Problem: can't have different backends, provider versions, or genuinely different configs per env. Separate roots: each env has own directory and state — true isolation. Recommendation: separate roots for prod/non-prod, workspaces for identical environments (multiple regions with same config).
bestPractices: Use separate directory roots for prod/non-prod environments, and workspaces for identical deployments (e.g. multi-region setups with identical configuration).

questions.question: What is a partial backend configuration?
questions.answer: Backend config split across main.tf (non-sensitive, committed) and -backend-config CLI flag (sensitive, not committed). Example: main.tf has bucket and region, -backend-config provides assume_role_arn. terraform init -backend-config=backend-prod.hcl. Enables different backends per environment from same code.
bestPractices: Use partial backend configurations to decouple sensitive backend credentials from codebase configuration.

questions.question: How do you structure Terraform for multiple environments?
questions.answer: Option 1: separate directories (environments/dev, environments/prod) — each calls shared modules. Option 2: Terragrunt — DRY wrapper with environment hierarchy. Option 3: workspaces (simple cases). Pattern: modules/ for reusable components, environments/ for instantiation. Never copy-paste code between environments.
bestPractices: Structure codebase with a modules/ directory for reusable elements, and environments/ for instantiation.
warnings: Never copy-paste configurations between environment folders.

questions.question: What backends does Terraform support?
questions.answer: Local: default, file on disk. S3: AWS, most common for teams. GCS: Google Cloud. AzureRM: Azure Blob. Terraform Cloud: remote state + execution + team features. HTTP: custom. Consul: HashiCorp. Use S3 + DynamoDB for AWS teams — battle-tested, simple, cheap, well-documented.
bestPractices: Use S3 + DynamoDB backends for AWS-centric engineering teams.

questions.question: What is Terraform Cloud and what does it add over open source?
questions.answer: Remote execution, remote state, team access controls, cost estimation, policy as code (Sentinel/OPA), audit logs, VCS integration (auto-plan on PR), private registry. Useful for: teams needing shared state without managing S3, policy enforcement, compliance audit. Free tier for small teams.

questions.question: How do you migrate from local to S3 backend?
questions.answer: Add backend 'S3' config to main.tf. Run terraform init — detects backend change and asks to copy state. Answer yes. Verify state in S3. Delete local terraform.tfstate. Commit backend config. Do not manually copy state files — let terraform init handle migration to avoid corruption.
warnings: Do not manually copy state files to the S3 bucket; let terraform init handle backend state migrations automatically.

questions.question: What is the issue with terraform destroy in a team environment?
questions.answer: Destroys ALL resources managed by that state — catastrophic if run on production. Mitigations: prevent_destroy on critical resources, separate state per environment, require multiple approvals for destroy in CI, never give developers terraform destroy access to production accounts.
bestPractices: Enforce prevent_destroy on critical assets.
Require multi-person approval for destroy operations in CI pipelines.
Never grant developers direct destroy permissions in production accounts.
warnings: terraform destroy will erase all infrastructure mapped in the state file. It is catastrophic if run on production.

questions.question: What is -target flag and why use it carefully?
questions.answer: Apply or plan only specific resources: terraform apply -target=aws_instance.web. Use for: recovering from partial failures, testing isolated changes. Risk: creates state inconsistencies — dependencies not applied. Never use -target as normal workflow. If using -target regularly, module boundaries are wrong.
warnings: Never use -target as part of a normal deployment workflow as it creates state inconsistencies.

questions.question: How do you handle secrets in Terraform?
questions.answer: Never hardcode in .tf files or commit to Git. Options: TF_VAR_ environment variables (from CI secrets), AWS Secrets Manager via data source, HashiCorp Vault provider, SSM Parameter Store. Mark variables sensitive=true. State file contains plaintext — encrypt with KMS. Restrict state bucket access strictly.
bestPractices: Mark variables carrying sensitive data as sensitive=true.
Restrict access to the state bucket strictly.
warnings: Never hardcode secrets in .tf files or commit them to Git repositories.
State files contain plaintext secrets; secure the S3 bucket and use KMS encryption.

questions.question: What security tools exist for Terraform?
questions.answer: tfsec: static analysis for misconfigurations (public S3, unencrypted EBS). Checkov: policy as code, 1000+ checks. Terrascan: compliance checks (PCI, HIPAA). Snyk IaC: vulnerability scanning. Sentinel/OPA: policy as code in Terraform Cloud. Run in CI before plan — catch misconfigs before AWS.
bestPractices: Run static scanning tools (tfsec, Checkov) in CI before the plan phase to catch misconfigurations prior to deployment.

questions.question: How do you prevent accidental resource deletion?
questions.answer: lifecycle prevent_destroy on critical resources. Separate state per environment. CI pipeline: plan output reviewed before apply. -target for surgical changes. Backend access controls. Git branch protection. For RDS: deletion protection at AWS level too. Multiple layers of protection for production data.
bestPractices: Configure deletion protection at the cloud provider level (e.g. RDS deletion protection) in addition to prevent_destroy.
Enable branch protection on repository main branches.

questions.question: What is least privilege for Terraform execution?
questions.answer: Terraform runner needs only permissions for resources it manages. Don't use AdministratorAccess. Create specific IAM role per Terraform workspace. Use permission boundaries. In CI: OIDC with GitHub Actions — no static AWS keys. Separate roles for plan (read-only) and apply (write).
bestPractices: Use OIDC with GitHub Actions to avoid static AWS credentials.
Create separate IAM roles for terraform plan (read-only) and terraform apply (write).
warnings: Do not grant AdministratorAccess to the Terraform execution runner role.

questions.question: How do you enforce Terraform coding standards in a team?
questions.answer: terraform fmt in pre-commit hook and CI. terraform validate in CI. tfsec/Checkov in CI. Required reviews on PRs for .tf changes. Module versioning policy. Naming conventions via custom validation. terraform-docs for documentation. Consistent variable naming (snake_case). README for every module.
bestPractices: Run terraform fmt and validation steps in pre-commit hooks and CI.
Require peer code reviews on all pull requests changing .tf files.
Provide a README file for every module using terraform-docs.

questions.question: What is Sentinel and OPA in Terraform context?
questions.answer: Policy as code frameworks. Sentinel (Terraform Cloud/Enterprise): enforces policies before apply — block resources without required tags, enforce instance type allowlist. OPA (Open Policy Agent): open source, flexible, integrates with Conftest for pre-plan checking. Both enforce guardrails beyond what IAM policies express.

questions.question: How do you manage provider credentials securely in CI?
questions.answer: GitHub Actions: OIDC with AWS — no static keys. assume_role in provider block — role assumed at runtime. Never store AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID in CI secrets. If static keys unavoidable: rotate frequently, least privilege, use secrets manager. Audit provider credential usage via CloudTrail.
bestPractices: Leverage OIDC with GitHub Actions to acquire short-lived credentials via IAM role assumption.
Audit credential usage logs using CloudTrail.
warnings: Never store AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID or AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY in CI/CD secrets directly.

questions.question: What is drift detection in Terraform?
questions.answer: Drift: real infrastructure differs from state (manual changes, external tools). Detect: terraform plan -refresh-only shows drift without proposing fixes. Automated: run plan in CI on schedule, alert on non-empty plans. Fix: terraform apply to revert, or import and update config. In GitOps: any drift is a policy violation.
bestPractices: Set up automated cron plans in CI to detect drift and trigger alerts.
Treat any infrastructure drift as a policy violation in GitOps.

questions.question: What are Terraform naming conventions and why do they matter?
questions.answer: Resources: snake_case, descriptive (aws_instance.web_server). Variables: snake_case, noun phrases. Outputs: snake_case, descriptive. Modules: noun phrases (vpc, eks_cluster). Files: main.tf, variables.tf, outputs.tf, versions.tf, locals.tf. Consistency enables grep, automation, onboarding. Enforced via team agreement and linting.
bestPractices: Adopt snake_case for resources, variables, outputs, and modules.
Consistently split configuration into standard files: main.tf, variables.tf, outputs.tf, versions.tf, and locals.tf.

questions.question: A plan shows a resource will be destroyed unexpectedly — investigate?
questions.answer: Read plan output: check + and - symbols. Reasons: resource name/type changed (forced replace), for_each key removed, dependency changed triggering replacement, provider upgrade changed behaviour. Use terraform plan -refresh=false to isolate config vs state diff. Check recent git changes to identify cause.

questions.question: How do you debug Terraform provider errors?
questions.answer: Set TF_LOG=DEBUG (or TRACE for maximum). TF_LOG_PATH=terraform.log writes to file. Shows raw HTTP requests/responses to provider API. Identify: auth errors, API rate limits, invalid parameters. Check provider changelog for breaking changes. Reproduce with minimal config. Open provider GitHub issue with debug log (redact secrets).
bestPractices: Set TF_LOG_PATH to write logs directly to a file for investigation.
warnings: Make sure to redact sensitive secrets/passwords from the debug log before publishing on GitHub issues.

questions.question: What happens if two team members run terraform apply simultaneously?
questions.answer: With DynamoDB locking: second apply waits for lock. If stuck: investigate before force-unlock. Without locking (local state): state corruption — both writes race, one overwrites the other, resources exist but untracked. Remote backend with locking is non-negotiable for team use — no exceptions.
warnings: Running without locking leads to race conditions, state corruption, and untracked resources.
Remote backend with locking is non-negotiable for team operations.

questions.question: How do you handle a provider API rate limit during apply?
questions.answer: Terraform retries automatically for transient errors. For persistent rate limiting: reduce parallelism with -parallelism=5 (default 10). Spread applies across time. Break monolithic config into smaller stacks. Check if provider has retry configuration. AWS: IAM and Route53 have aggressive rate limits.
bestPractices: Reduce the concurrency footprint by executing apply with a reduced parallelism limit.

questions.question: What is 'Error: Provider configuration not present'?
questions.answer: State has resources from a provider not in current config. Cause: provider removed but resources remain in state. Fix: add provider back temporarily, run terraform state rm for those resources, then remove provider. Or: terraform apply will offer to destroy orphaned resources. Always investigate before force-removing.
warnings: Always investigate why resources are orphaned in the state before force-removing them.

questions.question: How do you handle a failed apply that left resources in partial state?
questions.answer: Run terraform plan — Terraform reconciles partial state with desired config. Partial creates: retries remaining resources. Partial destroys: plan shows cleanup needed. Some resources may need manual cleanup (naming conflicts). Always run plan before next apply after failure. Use terraform state list to see what succeeded.
bestPractices: Always run terraform plan after a failed execution to see how Terraform intends to reconcile the state.

questions.question: What is 'Error acquiring the state lock'?
questions.answer: Another apply holds DynamoDB lock. First: confirm no apply is running. If stale: terraform force-unlock LOCK_ID. Risk: if apply IS running and you force unlock, concurrent applies corrupt state. Always verify before force-unlocking. Check CloudTrail for who started the locked apply.
warnings: Force unlocking while another apply execution is actively running will corrupt your state file.

questions.question: How do you upgrade Terraform version safely?
questions.answer: Check changelog for breaking changes. Test in dev first. Update required_version constraint. Run terraform init — may need provider upgrades. Run terraform plan — should show clean if no breaking changes. State format is usually forward-compatible. Never downgrade — state format may be incompatible with older versions.
bestPractices: Test version upgrades in development environments first.
warnings: Never downgrade Terraform versions after migrating state, as the state file format is not backward-compatible.

questions.question: What is the terraform graph command?
questions.answer: Outputs DOT format dependency graph of all resources. Visualise: terraform graph | dot -Tsvg > graph.svg. Useful for: understanding complex dependency chains, debugging unexpected ordering, explaining infrastructure. Large configs produce overwhelming graphs — filter with -type flag for targeted analysis.

questions.question: How do you split a large Terraform config into smaller stacks?
questions.answer: Identify natural boundaries: networking, compute, data, IAM — separate stacks. Use terraform_remote_state or SSM for cross-stack references. Apply order: foundational (VPC) → dependent (EKS) → application. Each stack has independent state, lifecycle, and permissions. Reduces blast radius and speeds up plan times significantly.
bestPractices: Deconstruct configurations along functional boundaries (VPC, databases, compute, IAM) into separate state files.
Adopt a strict apply hierarchy: foundational resources first, followed by consumers.

questions.question: Design a Terraform structure for a startup deploying dev/staging/prod on AWS.
questions.answer: Structure: modules/ (vpc, eks, rds, iam) + environments/ (dev/main.tf, staging/main.tf, prod/main.tf). Each env calls modules with env-specific vars. Separate S3 backend per env. GitHub Actions: plan on PR, apply on merge to main. Prod requires manual approval gate. Never auto-apply to production.
bestPractices: Organize using a flat modules + environment directory structure.
Configure a separate S3 backend per environment.
Enforce a PR-driven workflow requiring manual approval for production applies.
warnings: Never auto-apply plans directly to production environments without human review.

questions.question: A colleague ran terraform destroy on staging by mistake — what do you do?
questions.answer: Check prod is separate state — isolated. Assess staging damage. Rebuild: terraform apply from Git — IaC means rebuild is deterministic. Check RDS: if no prevent_destroy, restore from automated backup. Post-incident: add prevent_destroy to RDS, require approval for destroy, separate IAM role for staging lacking destroy permissions.
bestPractices: Post-incident: Enforce prevent_destroy on critical database resources.
Implement branch protections and restrict delete permissions in staging IAM roles.

questions.question: How would you onboard a new AWS account into your Terraform setup?
questions.answer: Create environment directory, configure S3 backend, create IAM role for Terraform OIDC. Bootstrap: apply baseline modules (VPC, IAM, logging, GuardDuty). PR-based workflow from day one. No manual console access. Account Factory for Terraform (AFT) for org-scale automation. IaC-first from account creation.
bestPractices: Bootstrap baseline modules immediately (VPC, IAM, cloud logging, GuardDuty).
Enforce zero manual console modifications from day one.
Use AWS Account Factory for Terraform (AFT) for automated organization scaling.

questions.question: Your terraform plan is taking 15 minutes — how do you speed it up?
questions.answer: Root cause: too many resources in one state (Terraform refreshes all on every plan). Solutions: split into smaller stacks (most effective). Use -target for urgent changes (tactical only). terraform plan -refresh=false skips refresh (risky). Upgrade provider version — some have optimised refresh. Reduce parallelism only if rate-limiting.
bestPractices: Break the monolithic configuration into multiple smaller state files to reduce API query times.
warnings: Running plan with -refresh=false skips API querying and can hide out-of-band changes (risky).

questions.question: How do you implement a tagging strategy with Terraform?
questions.answer: locals: common_tags = {Environment=var.env, Team=var.team, ManagedBy='terraform'}. Merge with resource-specific: tags = merge(local.common_tags, {Name='web-server'}). Module: accept additional_tags, merge inside. Enforce via: Checkov rule, AWS Config rule, SCP denying untagged resource creation.
bestPractices: Consolidate tags in a local block and merge them at the resource level.
Enforce tagging policies using static linter rules (Checkov) and organization policies (SCPs).

questions.question: A junior engineer committed AWS credentials to a .tf file in Git — response?
questions.answer: Immediate: rotate the credentials NOW — assume compromised. git filter-branch or BFG Repo Cleaner to remove from history. Force-push (coordinate with team). Check CloudTrail for usage since commit. Notify security. Add .gitignore rules. Add pre-commit hook: git-secrets or detect-secrets. Post-incident training.
bestPractices: Use BFG Repo Cleaner to erase the commit history containing credentials.
Implement git-secrets or detect-secrets in pre-commit hooks to block credential commits.
warnings: Committed keys must be assumed compromised; rotate them immediately.

questions.question: How do you implement blue/green infrastructure with Terraform?
questions.answer: Two identical resource sets (blue/green) using count or for_each. Traffic: Route53 weighted routing or ALB target group weights. Switch: update weight variable, apply. Keep old env until verified. Rollback: flip weights back. Terraform manages both in same state. Requires create_before_destroy on DNS/ALB resources.
bestPractices: Enable create_before_destroy on DNS and ALB routing records to facilitate smooth failovers.
Retain the inactive environment for a validation period before cleanup.

questions.question: How do you manage Terraform for 50+ AWS accounts in an organisation?
questions.answer: Atlantis or Terraform Cloud for remote execution. Directory per account or account type. Shared modules in private registry. Terragrunt for DRY configuration across accounts. Pipeline: PR triggers plan → approval → apply. SCP prevents resource creation outside Terraform. Drift monitoring on schedule.
bestPractices: Utilize Terragrunt to keep configuration DRY across multiple accounts.
Enforce an SCP blocking resource creation outside the Terraform execution role.
Schedule recurring drift detection jobs.

questions.question: Your module needs to support both AWS and GCP — how do you design it?
questions.answer: Provider-agnostic modules are generally an anti-pattern — abstractions leak. Better: separate module per provider with identical interface (variable names, output names). Wrapper module selects implementation based on var.cloud_provider. Don't force a common abstraction that makes both implementations worse.
bestPractices: Create a separate module per cloud provider with a matching interface.
Use a wrapper module that selects the provider-specific implementation based on a variable.
warnings: Provider-agnostic multi-cloud modules are an anti-pattern due to leaking abstractions.

questions.question: If you had to rebuild all infrastructure from Terraform tomorrow, what differently?
questions.answer: State isolation from day one. Modules for everything immediately — no copy-paste. OIDC for CI from start — no static keys ever. Terratest for module testing. Drift detection on schedule. Tagging enforced via policy. Private module registry. Smaller stacks. Document every non-obvious decision with comments. The best IaC is what the whole team can run without asking you.
bestPractices: Isolate state files and avoid copy-pasting code by creating modules immediately.
Implement OIDC and automate drift detection on schedule.
Document code thoroughly and test modules using Terratest.
